impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent holder's conditioning of patent licenses on customers' exclusive purchase of unpatented products constitutes unlawful tying under the Sherman Act, and whether the tied products had substantial non-infringing uses that would preclude antitrust liability.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed a jury verdict finding that Ingevity engaged in unlawful tying by conditioning licenses to its fuel vapor canister patent on customers' exclusive purchase of Ingevity's unpatented carbon honeycomb products. The court upheld the antitrust damages award, finding sufficient evidence that the tied products had substantial non-infringing uses beyond the patent's scope. This decision reinforces that patent holders cannot leverage patent rights to compel purchases of unpatented goods in adjacent markets.
impacts.positiveImplications: Competitors blocked from markets by patent-leveraged tying arrangements now have stronger precedent to challenge such practices and recover antitrust damages.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies with strong patent portfolios face increased antitrust risk when bundling licenses with product purchase requirements, even where the patent and product are commercially related.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that pharmaceutical method-of-treatment claims for humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for failure to satisfy the written description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed JMOL of invalidity of Teva's headache treatment patents, reinstating a jury verdict that Eli Lilly willfully infringed the patents covering methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headaches. The court found sufficient written description and enablement support in the specification's disclosure of prior-art methods for making and humanizing anti-CGRP antibodies. This is a major win for branded pharmaceutical patent holders in the lucrative migraine treatment market.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical companies benefit from confirmation that genus claims in biologic patents can be adequately supported by specification disclosures of known methods and a single species, reducing vulnerability to § 112 invalidity challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar manufacturers face stronger branded drug patent protection, potentially delaying market entry for competing migraine therapies.

impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to methods for detecting anomalous program executions by emulating programs and comparing function calls to a model are directed to abstract ideas under Alice step one, and whether damages may be awarded based on foreign sales of infringing software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict against Norton (Gen Digital), holding that Columbia's cybersecurity patents claiming methods for detecting anomalous program executions are abstract at Alice step one and require further step-two analysis on remand. The court also held that damages cannot be based on Norton's foreign sales. This decision narrows the scope of patent protection for software-based cybersecurity methods and limits extraterritorial patent damages.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies defending against software patent assertions benefit from stronger Alice step-one scrutiny of cybersecurity method claims and from the prohibition on foreign-sales-based damages.
impacts.negativeImplications: Universities and patent holders asserting software-related patents face heightened eligibility challenges and reduced damages potential when infringing products are sold globally.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court properly granted summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality where the accused multi-core processor selection method is performed partly outside the United States, and whether doctrine of equivalents theories were properly rejected.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed-in-part Intel's summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's multi-core processor patent, finding that genuine issues of material fact existed regarding whether Intel's accused process occurred within the United States and whether VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory was viable. The court also reversed the striking of VLSI's damages expert theories as an abuse of discretion. This decision clarifies the extraterritoriality analysis for method patents involving semiconductor design processes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting method patents against semiconductor companies benefit from a narrowed application of the extraterritoriality defense and protection of damages expert theories from premature exclusion.
impacts.negativeImplications: Semiconductor and technology companies face continued exposure to patent infringement claims even where significant design and manufacturing steps occur outside the U.S.

impacts.caseName: Global Tubing LLC v. Tenaris Coiled Tubes LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether summary judgment was properly granted on inequitable conduct claims based on alleged failure to disclose prior art during patent prosecution, and whether summary judgment was properly denied on Walker Process antitrust fraud claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment on both inequitable conduct and Walker Process antitrust fraud claims involving Tenaris's coiled tubing patents, finding genuine disputes of material fact on both issues. The court held that whether Tenaris deliberately withheld prior CYMAX documents from the patent office and whether such conduct amounted to antitrust fraud required resolution by a factfinder. This decision highlights the interplay between patent prosecution misconduct and antitrust liability.
impacts.positiveImplications: Competitors facing assertion of patents procured through potentially fraudulent prosecution have stronger grounds to pursue both inequitable conduct defenses and Walker Process antitrust counterclaims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders who acquired prior art through corporate acquisitions face heightened risk that failure to disclose such art during prosecution could support both patent unenforceability and antitrust liability.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony based on institutional knowledge (rather than personal knowledge) is admissible to establish prior sales for purposes of the on-sale bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b), and whether computer source code constitutes hearsay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating engine controller reprogramming patents under the on-sale bar, holding that 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony is admissible even when the witness lacks personal knowledge of the events and that computer source code is not hearsay. The court rejected the argument that the on-sale bar requires express disclosure of a device's functionality at the time of sale. This decision significantly strengthens defendants' ability to prove prior commercial sales using corporate designee testimony.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent challengers benefit from broader evidentiary tools to prove on-sale bar defenses, including corporate representative testimony based on company records rather than personal knowledge.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased invalidation risk where prior art products were sold commercially, even if no technical documentation was publicly available describing the product's internal functionality.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit issued a split decision on patent eligibility, vacating eligibility for certain constellation design patent claims while affirming eligibility for others, and affirmed both infringement and damages findings against LG Electronics. The court distinguished between claims reciting specific technical implementations of non-uniform constellations (eligible) and broader claims that merely recite the concept (requiring further analysis). This decision provides important guidance on the eligibility boundary for communications technology patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in communications technology benefit from confirmation that claims tied to specific technical implementations of signal processing innovations can survive § 101 challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: Consumer electronics manufacturers face continued patent liability exposure for implementing industry-standard communications technologies covered by valid patent claims.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement functionality violated Section 337 of the Tariff Act by infringing Masimo's wearable pulse oximetry patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 by importing Apple Watches that infringed Masimo's patents covering wearable blood oxygen measurement devices, upholding the limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing models. The court found no error in the Commission's domestic industry determination, validity rulings, or infringement findings. This high-profile decision has major implications for the wearable health technology market.
impacts.positiveImplications: Medical device and sensor technology patent holders have strong precedent for enforcing patents against major consumer electronics companies through ITC exclusion orders.
impacts.negativeImplications: Consumer electronics companies incorporating health-monitoring features face significant import exclusion risk when wearable health technology is covered by third-party patents.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB correctly construed claims related to streaming partly encrypted media content, affecting whether prior art renders the patent obvious.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the PTAB's claim construction in an inter partes review of DivX's streaming media encryption patent, vacating the Board's finding that Netflix failed to prove obviousness. The court adopted a different construction of the disputed claim terms and remanded for further proceedings. This decision impacts the streaming media industry by potentially invalidating patents covering adaptive bitrate streaming with partial encryption.
impacts.positiveImplications: Streaming service providers benefit from a more favorable claim construction that strengthens obviousness challenges to streaming encryption patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the digital media streaming space face increased vulnerability to IPR challenges based on corrected claim constructions.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTO Director's instructions governing discretionary denial of inter partes review institution constitute a 'general statement of policy' exempt from notice-and-comment rulemaking under 5 U.S.C. § 553(b).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the PTO Director's instructions to the PTAB on exercising discretion to deny IPR institution are general statements of policy exempt from notice-and-comment rulemaking requirements. The court held that because institution decisions are committed to the Director's unreviewable discretion and the instructions do not bind the Director, formal rulemaking is not required. This decision preserves the PTO's flexibility to adjust IPR institution policies without the procedural burdens of notice-and-comment rulemaking.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from confirmation that the PTO retains broad discretion to deny IPR institution through policy guidance rather than formal rules, potentially limiting challenges to issued patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies and patent challengers face reduced ability to contest PTO discretionary denial policies that limit access to the IPR system for challenging asserted patents.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court abused its discretion in excluding a patent plaintiff's damages expert report and subsequently granting summary judgment based on absence of a remedy.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report in a patent infringement suit against Microsoft involving virtual network optimization technology, vacating the subsequent summary judgment based on absence of a remedy. The court found that the district court applied an overly rigid standard in excluding the expert's damages methodology. This decision is significant for patent litigation practice, reinforcing that damages expert opinions should not be excluded merely for methodological imperfections that go to weight rather than admissibility.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent plaintiffs benefit from a more permissive standard for damages expert admissibility, reducing the risk that meritorious infringement cases are dismissed at summary judgment.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies defending patent suits face reduced ability to obtain early case dismissal through Daubert challenges to damages experts.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement over objections challenging subject matter jurisdiction, the fairness of the settlement, attorneys' fee awards, and incentive awards to class representatives.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed approval of a $125 million settlement resolving a nationwide class action alleging that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users by using fees to fund expenses unrelated to PACER operations. The court upheld the settlement's fairness, the attorneys' fee award, and incentive awards to the three nonprofit class representatives, rejecting all objections from a pro se objector. This decision affirms broad principles of class settlement approval and validates incentive awards to organizational class representatives.
impacts.positiveImplications: Class action plaintiffs and their counsel benefit from affirmation that incentive awards to organizational class representatives are permissible and that well-negotiated settlements following extensive litigation will be upheld.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether asserted trade secrets related to a cosmetic penile implant were legally protectable under California law where the information was generally known in the field, and whether the same publicly known information could constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed trade secret misappropriation verdicts and a permanent injunction, holding that the plaintiff failed to show its asserted trade secrets were protectable because the information was generally known in the industry. The court also reversed the denial of JMOL on patent invalidity, reasoning that information too generally known to qualify as trade secrets likewise cannot constitute inventive contributions for inventorship correction. This decision establishes an important doctrinal link between trade secret protectability and patent inventorship standards.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from strengthened requirements that plaintiffs demonstrate their information is not generally known, and from the principle that generally known information cannot support inventorship claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection face heightened evidentiary burdens to prove their information is truly secret, and risk losing both trade secret and patent claims simultaneously if the information is found to be generally known.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent that missed the statutory deadline for seeking a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) may obtain such a stay by voluntarily dismissing and refiling its district court declaratory judgment action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for obtaining a mandatory stay of parallel district court litigation by dismissing and refiling its declaratory judgment action. The court found that permitting such a maneuver would render the statutory deadlines in § 1659(a) meaningless. This decision is significant for pharmaceutical and other companies engaged in parallel ITC and district court patent proceedings, preventing strategic manipulation of the mandatory stay provision.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting claims in the ITC benefit from assurance that respondents cannot delay parallel district court proceedings indefinitely through strategic refiling to reset mandatory stay deadlines.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the 30-day mandatory stay deadline lose the ability to pause district court proceedings and must litigate on two fronts simultaneously.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB erred in its obviousness determination regarding sensor-based logistics patents, including the construction of claim limitations relating to restricting access to sensor information through predetermined time delays.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination invalidating FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent claims and remanded for further proceedings, finding errors in the Board's analysis. The case also raised issues about whether Qualcomm's IPR petition was an improper proxy filing on behalf of time-barred party Roambee. This decision is significant for supply chain technology companies and addresses the growing concern about third-party proxy IPR petitions designed to circumvent the one-year time bar.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in logistics and supply chain technology benefit from closer scrutiny of potentially proxy IPR petitions and from correction of PTAB analytical errors in obviousness determinations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking to challenge competitors' patents through IPR face increased risk that petitions filed near a related party's deadline will be scrutinized as potential proxy filings.
